walkthroughs.body_html:
Medieval doctors blamed illness on the four humours, God or bad air.

They used bleeding, purging and prayer. The Church protected Galen and banned dissection. Hospitals were run by monks and offered care, not cures.

In 1348 the plague reached England. People blamed God, miasma or Jews.

Treatments included herbs, lucky charms and flagellation. About one third of the population died. Towns began quarantine rules — an early sign of public health.

Printing and the Reformation weakened the Church's grip on knowledge.

Vesalius dissected criminals and published Fabric of the Human Body in 1543, correcting Galen. In 1628 Harvey proved the heart pumps blood round the body.

mcqs.q: Why was Vesalius significant in the history of medicine?
options: The four humours were invented by Pasteur to explain bacteria.
Vesalius invented the microscope.
His 1543 De Humani Corporis Fabrica corrected Galen's errors via human dissection and accurate illustration, founding modern anatomy though not curing disease.
Vesalius discovered the cause of disease and ended humoral theory.

mcqs.q: What was the theory of the four humours?
options: Medieval doctors knew about germs but used humours because they had no medicine.
The four humours were invented by Pasteur to explain bacteria.
Vesalius invented the microscope.
Disease was caused by imbalance of blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile; treatment aimed to rebalance them via bloodletting, purging or diet. It dominated for nearly 2,000 years.

mcqs.q: How did medieval people explain the Black Death?
options: Medieval people thought it was caused by germs they couldn't see.
Most blamed God's punishment for sin or bad air (miasma); some scapegoated Jews; doctors blamed planetary alignments and imbalanced humours.
Vesalius invented the microscope.
Medieval people knew it was spread by rats and fleas but had no way to stop it.
